title: Inquest hears 911 call made before Anthony Divers was shot by Hamilton police
subtitle: Coroner's jury hears recordings of Divers' estranged wife calling police after she was punched
article: A 911 call played for a coroner's jury into the police shooting death of Anthony Divers is from his estranged wife saying he just punched her and that he is a "dangerous offender."
Divers was shot dead soon after that call by a Hamilton police officer on James Street South.

"He's a dangerous offender ... he just punched me very badly across the face," his wife, Madeleine Divers, tells the 911 dispatcher on Sept. 30, 2016. "I'm in shock he'd come and punch me at my work ... He's really dangerous. I don't know if he has a gun."
She also says Divers was on crystal meth and fentanyl, and that he had a court order to not come within 500 feet of her.
The recording was heard Monday, Nov. 4, on the first day of an inquest into Divers' death.

Madeleine, a security guard at Club Seventy-Seven and Dirty Dog Saloon at the time of the shooting, refused to attend the inquest to testify. The jury instead heard her taped interview with the Special Investigations Unit (SIU), which investigates police shootings.

In it, she says she was outside her workplace - near Catharine Street North at King William in Hamilton's Beasley neighbourhood - when she saw Divers up the street. She approached him and told him he wasn't allowed to be there. She told the SIU his mental state was not good and she pleaded with him to go to St. Joseph's hospital for psychiatric help. That is when he punched her, she said.
The female officer who responded to the 911 call asked Madeleine if Divers had a gun.
"I specifically told her repeatedly he's not armed," Madeleine said. But she said the officer still radioed her police colleagues that Divers was possibly armed.
Madeleine said she could hear the officer's police radio when it broadcast "shots fired, shots fired."
"I freaked out," she said in the interview with the SIU.
She told the SIU that she had "called 911 so they could intervene and maybe get him to the hospital."
Madeleine said she and Divers had an argument earlier that day, where "he was hitting his own face. He said 'I can't take it anymore.'"
She also said he had a toy plastic gun that day, but did not have it that night outside her workplace.

An SIU report made public in August 2017 notes that Divers was not armed, but finds the police officer "reasonably believed that his life was in danger ... and his actions in firing upon Mr. Divers were justified."
The inquest heard first from Divers' oldest sister, Yvonne Alexander, who said "family was everything to Anthony."
Divers was the second of five siblings born in Canada of Scottish parents, and "he was such a loving child," she said.
But he was bullied as a teenager and fell in with the wrong crowd. He later served a penitentiary term for manslaughter and, afterwards, jail time for weapons offences.
Alexander said Divers blamed himself and the troubles he caused his family for his parents' death 36 days apart, both at age 65.
"Anthony felt their early death was his fault, that they were distraught over his being in jail."

She said Divers had been in hospital and at St. Joe's psychiatric unit on West 5th Street many times over the years and that he sometimes signed himself out of hospital, thinking he was well. He was discharged from hospital just days before his death, still in mental crisis, she said.
She last saw him two days before he died and he was "not in a good place." He was very distraught, didn't look well and had lost weight, she said.
She said he had never shown aggression toward police or his siblings. "The concern was he'd harm himself. Not anyone else."
Yvonne Hamilton, Divers' first wife, testified that Divers "was an amazing person, in every way. He was always loving and caring to me. He adopted my two girls."
She said the marriage ended because of his drug abuse, but that she continued to have contact him until the day he died.
"I still loved him," she said.
The inquest is scheduled to continue Tuesday. The inquest will examine the circumstances surrounding Divers' death. The jury might make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths.
An inquest is not a trial and does not attach blame or fault.
